prompt: For an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally and has no pulse, rescuers should

options.text: Begin high-quality CPR and use an AED as soon as available
Call for help and wait for EMS before starting compressions
Start with 2 rescue breaths, then begin compressions at 30:2
Check a pulse for up to 30 seconds before starting compressions

explanation: Adult cardiac arrest care prioritizes immediate compressions (starting CPR with chest compressions) and early defibrillation.

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for EMS delays compressions; every minute without CPR lowers the chance of survival.
distractorExplanations.c: Breaths-first (A-B-C) is the old sequence; current AHA adult CPR starts with compressions (C-A-B).
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse checks are limited to no more than 10 seconds before starting CPR, not up to 30 seconds.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: The recommended adult compression rate is

options.text: 40 to 50 per minute
100 to 120 compressions per minute
160 to 180 per minute
As slow as possible to avoid fatigue

explanation: AHA targets 100–120/min with adequate depth and full recoil.

distractorExplanations.a: Too slow reduces cardiac output support.
distractorExplanations.c: Too fast worsens depth/recoil.
distractorExplanations.d: Fatigue is managed by switching compressors ~every 2 minutes.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Adult compression depth should be at least

options.text: 1 inch (2.5 cm), not exceeding about 1.5 inches (4 cm)
1.5 inches (4 cm), not exceeding about 2 inches (5 cm)
2 inches (5 cm), not exceeding about 2.4 inches (6 cm)
3 inches (7.5 cm), not exceeding about 3.5 inches (9 cm)

explanation: Adequate depth is a key high-quality CPR metric; excessive depth can cause injury.

distractorExplanations.a: One inch is far too shallow; adult compressions need a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.b: About 1.5 inches (4 cm) is the infant depth target; adults need at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.d: Three inches exceeds the 2.4-inch (6 cm) upper limit for adults and raises the risk of injury.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Allowing complete chest recoil means:

options.text: Keeping light pressure on the sternum between compressions
Lifting the hands fully off the chest after each compression
Pausing about 2 seconds after each compression so the chest refills
Letting the chest return to normal position between compressions

explanation: Leaning reduces venous return; full recoil without leaning between compressions improves CPR quality.

distractorExplanations.a: Residual pressure (leaning) prevents full recoil and reduces venous return to the heart.
distractorExplanations.b: Hands stay in contact with the chest; lifting off risks losing hand position and bouncing.
distractorExplanations.c: Recoil happens within each compression cycle at 100-120/min; deliberate pauses drop the rate.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: The compression-to-ventilation ratio for single-rescuer adult CPR (without advanced airway) is

options.text: 100:0 always without exception

explanation: Without an advanced airway, adult CPR is 30 compressions to 2 breaths for one or two rescuers. After an advanced airway is in place, compressions are continuous and breaths are 1 every 6 seconds (10/min). 15:2 is the two-rescuer pediatric ratio, not adult.

distractorExplanations.b: 15:2 is the two-rescuer infant/child ratio without an advanced airway, not the adult ratio.
distractorExplanations.c: A 5:1 ratio is an old pediatric teaching point; current adult CPR without an advanced airway is 30:2.
distractorExplanations.d: Compression-only CPR is for untrained or unwilling rescuers; trained BLS providers give 30:2 when they can deliver breaths.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: When an AED arrives for an adult in cardiac arrest, you should?

options.text: Complete 5 cycles of CPR before attaching the pads
Power on the AED, apply pads, and follow prompts
Place both pads side by side on the left chest
Attach the pads and keep compressing while it analyzes

explanation: Early defibrillation is critical for shockable rhythms; minimize pauses and resume CPR immediately after a shock or no-shock advice.

distractorExplanations.a: Current guidance is to use the AED as soon as it arrives, not after a fixed number of CPR cycles.
distractorExplanations.c: Pads go in anterolateral (right upper chest, left side) or anteroposterior positions, not side by side.
distractorExplanations.d: Everyone must stand clear while the AED analyzes; compressions resume after the shock or no-shock prompt.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: If the AED advises “no shock,” the rescuer should

options.text: Check for a pulse for 10 seconds before resuming CPR
Give 2 rescue breaths, then reassess breathing
Resume CPR immediately starting with compressions
Turn off the AED and continue rescue breathing only

explanation: No-shock advice still requires high-quality CPR and reassessment per prompts.

distractorExplanations.a: After a no-shock prompt, resume compressions at once; rhythm and pulse are rechecked after about 2 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Breaths-first delays compressions; after the prompt, CPR resumes starting with compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: Pads and AED stay on to reanalyze every 2 minutes; a pulseless patient needs compressions, not breaths alone.

prompt: Hand position for adult compressions is

options.text: Heel of one hand on the upper half of the sternum, other on top
Heel of one hand on the xiphoid process, other hand on top
Two fingers on the sternum just below the nipple line
Heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top

explanation: Correct hand position (heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum, other hand on top) maximizes effective compressions and reduces injury risk.

distractorExplanations.a: The upper sternum is too high; compress on the lower half of the sternum in the center of the chest.
distractorExplanations.b: Pressing on the xiphoid can injure the liver; hands go on the lower half of the sternum above it.
distractorExplanations.c: Two-finger compressions are an obsolete infant method (dropped in 2025); adults use two hands, heel of one on the lower sternum.

prompt: To minimize interruption of chest compressions, rescuers should

options.text: Coordinate roles and switch compressors about every 2 minutes
Check a pulse after every cycle of 30 compressions and 2 breaths
Switch compressors only when the first rescuer feels tired
Stop compressions while the AED pads are being applied

explanation: High chest compression fraction improves outcomes; limit pulse/rhythm checks, and brief planned switches beat long chaotic pauses.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulse checks every cycle create frequent pauses; checks happen about every 2 minutes at rhythm analysis.
distractorExplanations.c: Fatigue lowers quality before rescuers notice it, so compressors switch about every 2 minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: Compressions continue while pads are applied; pause when the AED analyzes or delivers a shock.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: Rescue breaths for adults should

options.text: Be delivered over about 3 seconds each to fill the lungs
Produce visible chest rise over about 1 second each
Fill the lungs until the abdomen visibly rises
Be given as 10 breaths before starting compressions

explanation: Overventilation increases intrathoracic pressure and decreases venous return; avoid excessive ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Each breath should last about 1 second; longer breaths lengthen pauses in compressions.
distractorExplanations.c: Abdominal rise signals gastric inflation; give just enough volume for visible chest rise.
distractorExplanations.d: Prolonged breath-first sequences delay compressions; adult CPR uses 30:2 starting with compressions.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: For a witnessed adult collapse in a public place with a phone available, an alone rescuer should typically

options.text: Start CPR for 2 minutes before calling EMS or getting an AED
Check a pulse for 30 seconds, then call EMS and start CPR
Check responsiveness, activate EMS/get AED, then start CPR
Check responsiveness, give 2 breaths, then activate EMS

explanation: Rapid EMS activation and AED retrieval are core adult Chain of Survival links; ensure scene safety and check responsiveness and breathing first.

distractorExplanations.a: Two minutes of CPR before calling is for a lone rescuer with an unwitnessed child or infant arrest, not a witnessed adult collapse.
distractorExplanations.b: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds; a 30-second check delays EMS activation and compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: Breaths before activating EMS delay help and the AED; adult CPR then starts with compressions.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: If the victim has a medication patch on the chest where an AED pad will go, you should

options.text: Place the pad directly over the patch to save time
Delay the AED until EMS removes the patch safely
Wipe the patch with an alcohol pad and place the pad over it
Remove the patch and wipe the area dry

explanation: Patches can block energy and burn skin; remove the patch and wipe residue dry before applying the pad.

distractorExplanations.a: A pad over a medication patch can block energy delivery and cause skin burns.
distractorExplanations.b: Rescuers remove the patch themselves; waiting for EMS loses defibrillation time.
distractorExplanations.c: Wiping the surface does not remove the patch; it can still block current and cause burns.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: High-quality CPR includes limiting pauses ideally to:

options.text: Less than 10 seconds when possible for critical interventions
30–60 seconds routinely for convenience
No compressions until ALS arrives if ALS is 20 minutes away
Pauses after every single compression

explanation: Keep interruptions in compressions as short as possible — ideally under 10 seconds — so coronary perfusion pressure does not collapse. Rhythm checks and compressor switches happen about every 2 minutes, not as long pauses.

distractorExplanations.b: Pauses of 20–30 seconds wipe out coronary perfusion; compressions should resume within about 10 seconds.
distractorExplanations.c: BLS continues until ROSC, a valid DNR, or a trained team takes over — not a 10-second cap on the whole resuscitation.
distractorExplanations.d: The goal is continuous high-quality compressions with only brief pauses for shocks, analysis, or a compressor switch.

prompt: An adult with agonal gasps should be treated as:

options.text: Breathing adequately—place in the recovery position and monitor
Not breathing normally—start CPR if unresponsive and pulseless
Seizure activity—protect the head and wait for it to stop
An airway obstruction—begin abdominal thrusts at once

explanation: Agonal gasps are not adequate breathing and often occur in cardiac arrest.

distractorExplanations.a: Agonal gasps are not normal breathing; the recovery position would delay needed CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Gasping and brief jerking can follow cardiac arrest; treat it as not breathing, not as a seizure.
distractorExplanations.d: Agonal gasps signal cardiac arrest, not choking; abdominal thrusts are for responsive choking victims.

prompt: Team members should switch chest compressors approximately every

options.text: 30 seconds (or at each pause for breaths)
1 minute (or sooner if the compressor feels tired)
2 minutes (or when prompted by AED/team leader)
5 minutes (or when the AED prompts a shock)

explanation: Fatigue quickly degrades depth and rate; planned switches about every 2 minutes reduce fatigue and maintain quality.

distractorExplanations.a: Switching every 30 seconds adds needless pauses; the standard interval is about 2 minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Fatigue degrades quality before rescuers notice it; switch about every 2 minutes, not by feel.
distractorExplanations.d: Five minutes is too long; depth and rate fall off within about 2 minutes of compressing.

prompt: For child CPR (1 year to puberty), compression depth should be

options.text: About one-third the depth of the chest, approximately 2 inches (5 cm)
Shallow enough to avoid rib fractures, about one-quarter of the chest
The same 2.4-inch (6 cm) minimum used for adult compressions
About one-half the depth of the chest, approximately 3 inches (7.5 cm)

explanation: Pediatric depth targets ~⅓ chest depth (~2 inches in children)

distractorExplanations.b: Fear of rib fractures leads to shallow compressions; children need about one-third of chest depth.
distractorExplanations.c: 2.4 inches (6 cm) is the adult upper limit, not a minimum; children need about 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.d: One-half of chest depth is too deep and risks injury; the pediatric target is about one-third.

prompt: Two-rescuer CPR ratio for infants and children (without advanced airway) is commonly

options.text: 30:2 only

explanation: Without an advanced airway, two-rescuer infant or child CPR uses 15:2 so the extra pair of hands can share breaths. A lone rescuer still uses 30:2 for a child or infant. After an advanced airway, compressions are continuous.

distractorExplanations.a: 30:2 is the single-rescuer pediatric ratio; two rescuers switch to 15:2.
distractorExplanations.c: A 5:1 ratio is outdated pediatric teaching; two-rescuer infant/child CPR is 15:2.
distractorExplanations.d: 50:5 is not an AHA ratio; two rescuers use 15 compressions to 2 breaths.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: Infant chest compressions should be performed with which technique?

options.text: Two fingers on the sternum just below the nipple line
The heel of 1 hand, or 2 thumbs encircling the chest
Two stacked hands, as for an adult victim
Two fingers pressing on the xiphoid process

explanation: The 2025 AHA/AAP pediatric BLS guidelines dropped 2-finger compressions because they rarely reach adequate depth. Compress the lower sternum with the heel of 1 hand or the 2 thumb–encircling hands technique, about 1.5 inches (4 cm) or one-third of chest depth. If you cannot encircle the chest, use the heel of 1 hand. Skills testing now covers both allowed techniques.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-finger compressions were removed in the 2025 guidelines; they usually fail to reach 1.5 inches of depth.
distractorExplanations.c: Two stacked adult hands are too large and too deep for an infant chest and risk injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Pressing on the xiphoid risks liver injury; compress the lower half of the sternum just below the nipple line.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: Infant compression depth target is approximately

options.text: 0.5 inch (1 cm)
0.75 inch (2 cm)
1 inch (2.5 cm)
1.5 inches (4 cm)

explanation: Infant compression depth is about 1.5 inches (4 cm), or one-third of the chest’s anterior–posterior diameter, using heel of 1 hand or 2 thumbs. Adult depth (at least 2 inches / 5 cm) is too deep for an infant.

distractorExplanations.a: Half an inch is far too shallow to generate blood flow; infants need about 1.5 inches (4 cm).
distractorExplanations.b: Three-quarters of an inch is too shallow; the infant target is about one-third chest depth, 1.5 inches.
distractorExplanations.c: One inch underestimates the target; infant compressions should be about 1.5 inches (4 cm), one-third of chest depth.

prompt: If you are alone and find an unresponsive infant after an unwitnessed collapse, after ~2 minutes of CPR you should

options.text: Activate EMS/get AED if not already done, then continue CPR
Continue CPR without pausing until EMS arrives at the scene
Check a pulse for 30 seconds before deciding to call EMS
Give 5 back blows, then continue CPR before calling EMS

explanation: Pediatric sequences emphasize brief CPR before leaving to call if alone and collapse unwitnessed; follow current AHA course details for phone/AED steps.

distractorExplanations.b: No one has called EMS yet; after about 2 minutes of CPR the lone rescuer must activate EMS.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds; a 30-second check delays EMS activation and CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: Back blows are for a responsive choking infant, not an unwitnessed arrest; the next step is EMS.

prompt: For children, cardiac arrest is more often preceded by:

options.text: Sudden ventricular fibrillation than respiratory failure or shock
Respiratory problems / hypoxia than primary sudden cardiac causes
Congenital heart rhythm disorders than airway problems
Commotio cordis from chest impact than respiratory causes

explanation: Pediatric arrest is more often preceded by respiratory problems/hypoxia than primary sudden cardiac causes, though both occur; the Pediatric Chain of Survival emphasizes prevention and oxygenation, and compressions are still given for pulseless arrest.

distractorExplanations.a: VF is less common in children; most pediatric arrests follow respiratory failure or shock.
distractorExplanations.c: Congenital rhythm disorders cause some arrests, but respiratory failure and hypoxia are more common.
distractorExplanations.d: Commotio cordis is rare; pediatric arrest usually follows progressive respiratory failure.

prompt: When using an AED on a child, if pediatric pads/attenuator are unavailable?

options.text: Never defibrillate a child under any circumstance
Cut adult pads in half
Use adult pads; do not let pads touch each other
Place both adult pads stacked on the umbilicus

explanation: Adult AEDs may be used if pediatric system unavailable; pad placement must not overlap.

distractorExplanations.a: Shockable pediatric rhythms need defibrillation.
distractorExplanations.b: Do not modify pads by cutting.
distractorExplanations.d: Follow anteroposterior or standard positions as trained.

prompt: Infant rescue breaths should

options.text: Be quick cheek puffs without watching for chest rise
Fill the infant's lungs until the abdomen rises
Be delivered over about 3 seconds each
Be gentle enough to produce chest rise

explanation: Overventilation is harmful; visible chest rise is the guide. With mouth-to-mouth-and-nose, the rescuer's mouth covers the infant's mouth and nose.

prompt: Pulse check location commonly taught for infants is

options.text: Brachial artery
Radial artery only as first choice
Popliteal
Carotid only as the sole infant site taught

explanation: Brachial pulse is standard for infants; carotid/femoral used in older children.

distractorExplanations.b: Radial is difficult in infants.
distractorExplanations.c: Popliteal not the standard infant check.
distractorExplanations.d: Carotid is more for children/adults.

prompt: For a child who is unresponsive and not breathing normally but has a pulse ≥60/min with poor perfusion signs, BLS may include

options.text: Full CPR at 15:2 now, since the child is unresponsive and not breathing
Rescue breathing, and start compressions if pulse remains <60 with poor perfusion
Rescue breathing at 1 breath every 6 seconds, starting compressions only if pulse is lost
Recovery position and monitoring until EMS arrives, with no breaths given

explanation: Pediatric bradycardia with poor perfusion is a compression indication even if a pulse is present but too slow; give rescue breathing with pulse checks per AHA pediatric guidance.

distractorExplanations.a: With a pulse of 60 or more, give rescue breaths; compressions start if it falls below 60 with poor perfusion.
distractorExplanations.c: Pediatric rescue breathing is 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, and compressions start below 60 with poor perfusion, not on pulse loss.
distractorExplanations.d: A child who is not breathing normally needs rescue breaths; the recovery position is for adequate breathing.

prompt: When should the 2 thumb–encircling hands technique be used for infant compressions?

options.text: Only when two rescuers are present; a lone rescuer must use two fingers
Whenever the rescuer can encircle the chest; otherwise use the heel of 1 hand
Never — only the heel of 1 hand is permitted after 2025
Only during choking when the infant still has an effective cough

explanation: 2025 AHA BLS allows either the heel of 1 hand or 2 thumb–encircling hands for infant compressions. Use thumbs when you can encircle the chest; if you cannot, use the heel of 1 hand. Two-finger compressions are no longer recommended, even for a lone rescuer.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-finger technique is no longer taught; a lone rescuer uses the heel of 1 hand if they cannot encircle the chest.
distractorExplanations.c: Both heel-of-1-hand and 2 thumb–encircling hands are recommended; thumbs are not banned.
distractorExplanations.d: An infant with an effective cough is still a mild obstruction — observe and encourage coughing, do not start compressions.

prompt: Compression rate for infants and children is

options.text: 40 to 60 per minute
60 to 80 per minute
80 to 100 per minute
100 to 120 per minute

explanation: Infants and children use the same compression rate as adults: 100–120 per minute, with full recoil. Rate does not slow just because the patient is small.

distractorExplanations.b: 60-80/min is too slow; infants and children get the same 100-120/min rate as adults.
distractorExplanations.c: 80-100/min is below target; the pediatric compression rate matches adults at 100-120/min.

prompt: If a child has a pulse and is breathing adequately after a brief seizure, you should

options.text: Protect airway, place recovery position if appropriate, and monitor
Begin chest compressions because a seizure can stop the heart
Place a bite block in the mouth to protect the tongue
Give sips of water to prevent dehydration once the seizure has ended

prompt: For infant CPR landmarking, compressions are delivered

options.text: On the lower tip of the sternum (xiphoid)
Just below the nipple line on the sternum
On the upper third of the sternum near the neck
On the left chest over the heart

distractorExplanations.d: Compressions go on the sternum, not the left chest; the heart is compressed between sternum and spine.

options.text: Cut adult pads in half so both fit on the front of the chest
Overlap the pads slightly so both fit on the front of the chest
Ensure pads do not touch (use AP placement if needed on small chests)
Skip the AED for children under 8 years if pediatric pads are not available

prompt: A responsive adult with severe choking (cannot speak or cough effectively) needs

options.text: Cycles of 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts until the object expels or the person is unresponsive
Encouraging forceful coughing and waiting for the object to clear itself
A blind finger sweep to find the object, then abdominal thrusts only
Rescue breaths to push the object past the airway

explanation: 2025 AHA adult FBAO: for severe obstruction, give repeated cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the person becomes unresponsive. options.text: Give naloxone first and wait 2 minutes before starting CPR
Give rescue breaths and naloxone, but skip the AED in an overdose arrest
Start CPR and use AED; administer naloxone without delaying compressions
Start CPR but withhold the AED until naloxone has been given

explanation: Cardiac arrest care still follows CPR/AED; naloxone is adjunctive, given as soon as available, and is not a reason to skip BLS.

distractorExplanations.a: In pulseless arrest CPR starts at once; naloxone must not delay compressions.
distractorExplanations.b: Opioid-associated arrests can have shockable rhythms; use the AED as in any arrest.
distractorExplanations.d: The AED is applied as soon as it arrives; naloxone must not delay defibrillation.

prompt: Naloxone (intranasal/autoinjector) in BLS settings is intended to:

options.text: Reverse low blood sugar in a person found unresponsive
Permanently reverse an overdose so EMS is not needed
Reverse respiratory depression from any sedative drug
Temporarily reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression

explanation: Effects may wear off; monitor and be ready to redose per protocol; continue airway support.

distractorExplanations.a: Low blood sugar is treated with glucose; naloxone reverses opioid effects, not hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.b: Naloxone wears off, often before the opioid does, so EMS care is still needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone is opioid-specific; it does not reverse benzodiazepines, alcohol, or other sedatives.

prompt: After successful naloxone response, the person may

options.text: Become agitated or re-sedate later as naloxone wears off
Be released without EMS once awake for 15 minutes
Stay alert, since naloxone lasts longer than most opioids do
Safely drive home once breathing returns to normal

explanation: Renarcotization is a known risk; observation is mandatory, so continue observation and EMS care.

distractorExplanations.b: Re-sedation can occur after naloxone wears off; the person needs ongoing observation and EMS care.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone's effect often ends before long-acting opioids do, so re-sedation is a real risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Re-sedation can follow as naloxone wears off; the person should not drive and needs observation.

prompt: A choking child who becomes unresponsive should receive

options.text: Abdominal thrusts while kneeling astride the child
CPR with checks for visible objects before breaths
Back blows and chest thrusts while lying on the floor
Blind finger sweeps before each set of compressions

explanation: Same transition to CPR as adults/children when unresponsive from FBAO.

distractorExplanations.a: Astride abdominal thrusts are not taught; an unresponsive choking child gets CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: Back blows and chest thrusts are for responsive choking infants, not an unresponsive child.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only objects you can see.

prompt: Signs of severe foreign-body airway obstruction include

options.text: Loud forceful coughing with the ability to speak in full sentences
Noisy wheezing between strong, effective coughs
Inability to speak, weak/silent cough, universal choking sign
Hoarse voice, strong cough, and normal skin color

explanation: Differentiate mild vs severe to choose observation vs thrusts; severe signs also include cyanosis.

distractorExplanations.a: Forceful coughing and full speech mean air is moving: mild obstruction, so encourage coughing.
distractorExplanations.b: Wheezing between effective coughs indicates mild obstruction; keep encouraging the victim to cough.
distractorExplanations.d: A strong cough with normal color and voice is mild obstruction; severe means no effective air movement.

prompt: For pregnant choking victims, hand position for chest thrusts is

options.text: Just above the navel, below the ribs
On the xiphoid process
Upper third of the sternum
Center of the sternum

explanation: Chest thrusts avoid the gravid abdomen; hands go in the same general area as CPR compressions, per BLS training details.

distractorExplanations.a: Just above the navel is the abdominal-thrust position, which compresses the gravid uterus.
distractorExplanations.b: Pressing on the xiphoid risks liver injury; chest thrusts use the center of the sternum.
distractorExplanations.c: The upper sternum is too high; hands go on the center of the sternum, like CPR compressions.

prompt: Scene safety with suspected opioid overdose includes:

options.text: Use PPE as trained and avoid needle sticks
Delaying care until hazmat clears skin-contact risk
Wearing an N95 respirator before touching the victim
Recapping found needles before moving the victim

explanation: Rescuers protect themselves while providing rapid care; know fentanyl exposure myths vs real risks. Incidental skin contact is not the main danger; avoid mucous membrane/sharps exposure.

distractorExplanations.b: Incidental skin contact with fentanyl is very low risk; delaying care for hazmat costs critical time.
distractorExplanations.c: Routine respirators are not needed for overdose response; standard PPE and sharps care suffice.
distractorExplanations.d: Recapping needles is a leading cause of needle-stick injury; leave sharps alone or use a sharps container.

prompt: High-flow oxygen / advanced airway management beyond BLS scope should be

options.text: Done by any BLS rescuer with an airway kit
Left to trained ALS providers
Started before chest compressions begin
Given priority over early AED use

explanation: Know your scope; BLS focuses on basic ventilation and compressions, and high-quality BLS bridges to ALS.

distractorExplanations.a: Advanced airways need ALS training and credentials; BLS uses bag-mask or mouth-to-mask ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressions come first; advanced airway placement must not delay CPR.
distractorExplanations.d: Early defibrillation outranks advanced airway placement in the BLS sequence.

prompt: If the first cycle of back blows and abdominal thrusts does not clear a responsive adult’s severe choking, you should

options.text: Switch to rescue breaths to force the object down
Stop the maneuvers and wait for EMS while the victim tries to cough
Continue alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
Do a blind finger sweep after each unsuccessful cycle

explanation: Keep repeating 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the adult becomes unresponsive. Then lower them to a firm surface, start CPR, and look for a visible object before each breath.

distractorExplanations.a: Rescue breaths are for unresponsive victims during CPR; a responsive victim needs continued back blows and thrusts.
distractorExplanations.b: A victim who cannot cough effectively still needs the FBAO cycles, not a pause while waiting for EMS.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind sweeps can lodge the object deeper; look for and remove only an object you can see.

prompt: Closed-loop communication means:

options.text: The receiver repeats back the order and the sender confirms
The sender repeats the order twice so everyone hears it
The receiver nods and starts the task without speaking
Each team member reports status to the leader at set intervals

explanation: Closed-loop communication: the sender gives an order, the receiver repeats it back, and the sender confirms. That read-back catches wrong drugs, doses, and missed tasks in a noisy code.

distractorExplanations.b: Repeating an order is one-way; closed loop needs the receiver to echo it and the sender to confirm.
distractorExplanations.c: A nod gives no verbal check; closed loop requires a read-back and confirmation.
distractorExplanations.d: Scheduled reports are status updates; closed loop confirms each order as it is given.

prompt: A team leader’s role includes:

options.text: Doing chest compressions personally while directing the team
Assigning roles, monitoring CPR quality, and summarizing the plan
Managing the airway while directing the other roles
Waiting for team members to choose their own roles

explanation: Leadership improves coordination and chest compression fraction.

distractorExplanations.a: The leader stays hands-off to oversee the whole resuscitation and CPR quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Airway management is a team member role; a hands-on leader loses oversight.
distractorExplanations.d: The leader assigns roles; letting members self-select causes gaps and duplication.

prompt: Constructive intervention means a team member should

options.text: Report the error to the team leader at the debrief afterward
Quietly correct the error without telling the leader
Speak up clearly if a critical error is about to occur
Wait until the leader asks for team input

explanation: Safety culture expects respectful challenge of dangerous actions; speak up when a critical error or unsafe action is about to occur.

distractorExplanations.a: Critical errors must be addressed in real time; the debrief is too late to protect the patient.
distractorExplanations.b: Silent corrections bypass the leader and closed-loop communication; state the concern clearly.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for permission lets an unsafe action happen; speak up immediately.

prompt: During CPR with an advanced airway in place, ventilations are typically given

options.text: 2 breaths after every 15 compressions, pausing for each
2 breaths after every 30 compressions, as without an airway
1 breath every 6 seconds, pausing compressions for each
1 breath every 6 seconds with continuous compressions

explanation: An advanced airway allows continuous compressions with timed breaths: 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min) without 30:2 pauses.

distractorExplanations.a: 15:2 with pauses is two-rescuer child/infant CPR without an advanced airway.
distractorExplanations.b: 30:2 is for CPR without an advanced airway; with one in place, compressions are continuous.
distractorExplanations.c: With an advanced airway, compressions do not pause for breaths; ventilation is asynchronous.

prompt: Pregnant patient in cardiac arrest: in addition to high-quality CPR, rescuers should

options.text: Perform manual left uterine displacement to relieve aortocaval compression
Perform manual right uterine displacement to relieve vena cava pressure
Withhold AED shocks to protect the fetus until obstetric help arrives
Move hand position 2 inches lower on the sternum for compressions

explanation: LUD improves venous return when the uterus is clinically significant; defibrillation is still indicated when needed; maternal resuscitation prioritizes CPR.

distractorExplanations.b: Displacement is to the left, moving the uterus off the aorta and inferior vena cava.
distractorExplanations.c: Defibrillation is safe and indicated in pregnancy; withholding shocks harms mother and fetus.
distractorExplanations.d: Compression hand position is the same as for other adults, on the lower half of the sternum.

prompt: If a rescuer is too fatigued to keep correct compression depth, the best action is

options.text: Keep going until the 2-minute rhythm check, then switch
Announce the need to switch and rotate immediately
Slow the rate to 90 per minute to keep the depth
Use one hand to rest the other while compressing

explanation: Teamwork corrects fatigue; announce the switch and rotate with minimal pause, since pride should not degrade CPR quality.

distractorExplanations.a: A fatigued compressor delivers shallow compressions; switch now rather than waiting for the check.
distractorExplanations.c: Rate must stay at 100-120/min; trading rate for depth still lowers CPR quality.
distractorExplanations.d: Adult compressions need two hands to reach adequate depth; resting one hand reduces depth further.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 2).

prompt: Using a bag-mask device effectively usually requires:

options.text: Squeezing the bag fully and quickly for each breath
One-rescuer use, which gives the best mask seal
Proper seal and often two-person technique
A mask sized to cover the chin and the eyes

explanation: Seal and airway position determine tidal delivery; two-person technique gives better ventilation. Avoid overventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Full, fast squeezes overinflate and cause gastric inflation; give just enough for chest rise over 1 second.
distractorExplanations.b: Two-rescuer bag-mask ventilation gives a better seal than the one-rescuer technique.
distractorExplanations.d: The mask covers the nose and mouth, from the bridge of the nose to the cleft of the chin, not the eyes.

prompt: When to stop BLS efforts is generally determined by:

options.text: Personal inconvenience after 1 minute
Family requesting social media posts first
Guessing without assessment that “it’s fine”
Obvious signs of life/ROSC, transfer to ALS, valid DNR orders meeting local rules, or scene becoming unsafe

explanation: Know local protocols and legal/ethical frameworks for termination/withholding.

distractorExplanations.a: 1 minute is far too early.
distractorExplanations.b: Social media is irrelevant.
distractorExplanations.c: Assessment drives decisions.

prompt: Special situation: victim on a soft bed—for CPR you should

options.text: Move the victim to a firm surface
Compress harder to make up for the soft mattress
Switch to rescue breaths until a backboard arrives
Compress at a faster rate to offset the mattress

explanation: Soft surfaces dissipate force; move the victim to a firm surface or place a backboard if available to improve compression effectiveness.

distractorExplanations.b: Extra force on a soft surface is absorbed by the mattress; firm support is needed for effective depth.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressions must continue; moving to a firm surface takes priority over breaths-only care.
distractorExplanations.d: A faster rate does not fix lost depth on a mattress; 100-120/min stays the target rate.

prompt: If the victim has a hairy chest and AED pads will not stick

options.text: Press the pads firmly over the hair and analyze
Quickly remove hair in the pad area so pads adhere
Move both pads to the back where there is less hair
Delay the AED and continue CPR until EMS arrives

explanation: Pad contact is required for AED function; kits often include a razor, so remove hair in the pad area, then analyze.

distractorExplanations.a: Pads over thick hair make poor contact, causing failed analysis or skin burns.
distractorExplanations.c: Both pads on the back do not create a correct current path through the heart.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying defibrillation lowers survival; clear the hair and use the AED.

prompt: Water/scene: before AED use on a victim in a wet environment

options.text: Apply the pads to the wet chest, as AEDs are water-safe
Dry only the pad sites, leaving the victim in the water
Move to a dry area if possible and dry the chest
Turn the victim onto the side to drain water first

explanation: Reduce shock hazard to rescuers by avoiding standing water; AEDs are used after reasonable drying/movement.

distractorExplanations.a: Water conducts current across the chest and toward rescuers, so the chest must be dried first.
distractorExplanations.b: Leaving the victim in standing water risks shocking rescuers; move to a dry area first.
distractorExplanations.d: Draining water from the lungs delays CPR and AED use and is not part of BLS.

prompt: Role clarity during a code is improved when each member

options.text: Rotates freely between tasks as needs arise
Takes direction from whoever is closest to the patient
Chooses a task after first seeing which roles are already covered
Knows their assignment and stays in lane unless reassigned

explanation: Clear roles (compressions, airway, AED, documentation) prevent task fixation and missed compressions.

distractorExplanations.a: Free rotation causes gaps; members take assigned roles and switch on the leader's call.
distractorExplanations.b: Direction comes from one designated team leader, not from proximity to the patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Self-selecting roles causes gaps and duplication; the leader assigns roles.

prompt: Feedback devices / CPR coaches help teams by:

options.text: Prompting rate, depth, recoil, and pauses in real time
Analyzing the heart rhythm and advising a shock
Reporting CPR quality only at the post-event debrief
Setting the ventilation volume for the bag-mask

explanation: Quality metrics improve with coaching and feedback tools when available.

distractorExplanations.b: Rhythm analysis is the AED's job; feedback devices measure compression quality.
distractorExplanations.c: Feedback devices coach in real time during CPR; debrief data is a secondary use.
distractorExplanations.d: Feedback devices focus on compressions and pauses, not on setting bag-mask volume.

prompt: For a victim with a tracheostomy who needs ventilation, BLS-trained providers should

options.text: Ventilate through the mouth and nose as in other adults
Ventilate via the tracheostomy using appropriate interface as trained
Remove the tracheostomy tube first, then ventilate by the mouth and nose
Skip ventilation and give compression-only CPR instead

explanation: Ventilate the airway the patient has; follow training for stoma ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Breathing occurs through the stoma; mouth breaths will not reach the lungs effectively.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the tube can close the airway; ventilate through the tracheostomy.
distractorExplanations.d: Trained providers ventilate through the stoma; skipping breaths loses oxygenation.

prompt: After ROSC (return of spontaneous circulation), BLS providers should

options.text: Remove the AED pads and sit the patient upright to help them breathe
Continue compressions for 2 more minutes to prevent re-arrest
Support airway/breathing, monitor pulse, and prepare for ALS care
Give sips of water once the patient begins to respond to voice

explanation: Re-arrest is common; continue close monitoring of pulse and blood pressure as able, with supportive care, and prepare for transport/ALS care.

distractorExplanations.a: Pads stay on after ROSC because re-arrest is common and may need another shock.
distractorExplanations.b: Compressions on a patient with a pulse are not indicated; monitor and support instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Oral fluids risk aspiration after ROSC; nothing by mouth while consciousness is altered.
